intro: Japan is a long chain of islands on the Pacific Ring of Fire. Mountains and volcanoes cover most of it, so its people crowd onto narrow coastal plains, and earthquakes are part of everyday life.

chapters.title: A country of islands
text: Japan is made of more than 14,000 islands. Four main islands hold most people: Honshu, the largest, with Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto; Hokkaido in the snowy north; and Kyushu and Shikoku in the south-west. The Okinawa islands stretch further south towards Taiwan.
Its nearest neighbours across the sea are South Korea, China and Russia, and Japan has unresolved disputes with each of them over small islands.

chapters.title: Mountains and volcanoes
text: About three-quarters of Japan is mountainous, so cities, farms and factories are packed into the flat land along the coasts. The Japanese Alps run down the middle of Honshu.

Japan sits where four of Earth's tectonic plates meet, on the Pacific Ring of Fire. It has more than 100 active volcanoes. Mount Fuji, its highest and most famous mountain, is a volcano that last erupted in 1707.

highlight.title: Shaking ground
highlight.text: About a fifth of the world's strongest earthquakes happen in or near Japan. Buildings are designed to sway rather than collapse, and schoolchildren practise earthquake drills. 'Tsunami' is a Japanese word.

chapters.title: From snow to coral
text: Because Japan stretches so far from north to south, its climate ranges from cold and snowy in Hokkaido, where winters are like Canada's, to warm and subtropical in Okinawa, with coral reefs. The mountains facing the Sea of Japan get some of the heaviest snowfalls of any inhabited place on Earth.

Most of Japan has four clear seasons. A rainy season comes in early summer, and typhoons can strike in late summer and autumn. Spring cherry blossoms are so important that the news reports a daily 'blossom front' as they open from south to north.

chapters.title: Forests and wildlife
text: Despite its huge cities, Japan is one of the most forested countries in the developed world, with forests covering about two-thirds of the land.
Japanese macaques, known as snow monkeys, live further north than any other monkey and famously bathe in hot springs in winter. Tame deer wander the streets of the old city of Nara.

places.title: Landscape tour
places.intro: Places that show the variety of Japan's landscapes. The numbers match the pins on the map.

items.name: Mount Fuji
items.text: Japan's highest and most famous mountain, a nearly perfect volcanic cone.

items.name: Japanese Alps
items.text: High, snowy peaks in the middle of Honshu.

items.name: Jigokudani
items.text: Where snow monkeys bathe in hot springs in winter.

items.name: Shiretoko
items.text: A remote peninsula in Hokkaido with brown bears and winter sea ice.

items.name: Matsushima Bay
items.text: More than 200 pine-covered islets, one of Japan's three most famous views.

items.name: Lake Biwa
items.text: Japan's largest lake, one of the oldest lakes in the world.

items.name: Tottori Sand Dunes
items.text: Huge sand dunes on the Sea of Japan coast.

items.name: Mount Aso
items.text: An active volcano inside one of the largest calderas on Earth.

items.name: Yakushima
items.text: Mossy forests with cedar trees thought to be thousands of years old.

items.name: Kerama Islands
items.text: Turquoise water and coral reefs in Okinawa.
